blocks.text: Since a man most learned in Hebrew ^{(4)} saw that the common interpretation was pressed by these difficulties, he thought that the words of Jeremiah could be rendered thus: The partridge gathered (or [II, 642] warmed eggs), but did not bring forth, that is, did not hatch the eggs. Several reasons could be given why it happens to the partridge more often than to any other bird that it warms eggs which it does not hatch. The first is that it nests neither on rocks, nor on the branches of trees, nor on the tops of towers, but on the ground, in a place most exposed not only to fowlers but also to wild beasts and reptiles. The second is that if the partridge's eggs become wet from falling dew or rain, ἐὰν μὴ πάλιν ἡ τεκοῦσα ἐπιθάλψῃ αὐτὰ ἐπελθοῦσα ταχέως, γίνεται ἄγονα [ean mē palin hē tekousa epithalpsē auta epelthousa tacheōs, ginetai agona], unless the mother at once sits on them and warms them again, they are rendered infertile. So Aelian, book 10, ch. 35 of the Hist. animal. The third lies in the males, which through unrestrained lust sometimes break the eggs, so that the females may not be detained too long by incubating. Besides Aelian ^{e)}, this is reported by Aristotle ^{f)}, Pliny ^{g)}, Athenaeus ^{h)} and Philes ^{i)}. But one thing stands against the interpretation we have described: the verb to bring forth in Jeremiah refers not to ἐκλέπισιν [eklepisin], but to ὠοτοκίαν [ōotokian], which everyone knows to be very different from hatching. The matter is perfectly plain in the passage of Isaiah we have cited about the serpent acontias: There the acontias will nest, and lay, and break, that is, hatch the eggs, which are broken in hatching. Among the Hebrews, therefore, in oviparous animals laying is one thing and hatching another. Laying is ὠοτοκία [ōotokia], and is expressed by the verbs ילד and מלט, as hatching is by the verb בקע, which means to break. Thus the passage of Jeremiah, the kore gathered, and did not bring forth, must be taken as it sounds, so that it is understood of a bird that warms eggs laid by another. This is something the naturalists nowhere ascribe to the partridge, but only the Fathers do.

R. Selomo is not consistent. For on Samuel he holds קרא kore to be the partridge, as other Hebrews do. But on Jeremiah he interprets it as the cuckoo, because many think it is peculiar to the cuckoo to sit on other birds' eggs. This opinion had long ago become established among the common people of the French (the nation among whom Selomo lived 550 years ago). Hence even today in common speech the French call cuckoo, as an insult, a man whose wife is an adulteress, because he unknowingly cherishes and rears another's children. Carried away by the same popular error, Acron, a distinguished grammarian, writes thus on the cuckoo, on Horace book 1, Sat. 7: The cuckoo bird suffers from this natural defect: forgetting where it has laid its eggs, it often warms those of others; hence rustics taunt one another with it, as if bearing the care of another's offspring. [col. 88] But in truth the matter is entirely otherwise. For the cuckoo does not sit on others' eggs, but lays in another's nest and hands over its eggs to other birds to be incubated and hatched. Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 29: Ὁ δὲ κόκκυξ οὐ ποιεῖ νεοττίαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ἀλλοτρίαις τίκτει νεοττίαις [Ho de kokkyx ou poiei neottian, all᾽ en allotriais tiktei neottiais]. Likewise: Ἐπωάζει δὲ οὐκ αὐτὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν οὗ ἂν τέκῃ νεοττίᾳ, οὗτος ὁ ὄρνις ἐκκολάπτει καὶ τρέφει [Epōazei de ouk autos, all᾽ en hou an tekē neottia, houtos ho ornis ekkolaptei kai trephei]. Theophrastus [II, 643] ^{k)}, Antigonus of Carystus ^{l)}, Pliny ^{m)}, Aelian ^{n)}, Oppian ^{o)}, Philes ^{p)} and others of the ancients teach the same at greater length. Among the Hebrews too, Rabbi Gersom in Porta coeli, fol. 30, ch.: ואומר על עוף שנקרא קוג"ול שאינו מחמם ביציו אך מניח אותם בתוך קנים של שאר עופות ואותם עופות חשובים שהם ביציהם The bird which they call the cuckoo does not warm its own eggs, as they say, but places them in the nests of other birds; and those birds think these eggs are their own. And experience, the teacher of things, attests that this is so. Accordingly, in the Roman tongue a cuculus [cuckoo] is not the man who suffers the insult from his wife, but the one who inflicts it. In a word, the cuckoo is the same as the adulterer, because the adulterer, like the cuckoo, lies in a nest not his own. Hence Artemona, the woman in Plautus' Asinaria, greets her husband Demaenetus, caught in the brothel with a harlot ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρῳ [ep’ autophōrō], with this insult:
Grey-headed cuckoo, your wife drags you home from the dens of vice.
But the man whom we French call a cuculus [cuckoo], the Romans called a curruca. Juvenal, Satire 6, of a stupid husband pitying the false tears of his adulterous wife:
You now, curruca, are pleased with yourself, and sip up her weeping with your lips. — — — — —
